prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby showing how trade reallocates resources across firms and shapes productivity and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: one part, B010, credited to Melitz and Helpman. The round-1 exchange sharpened my reasons but did not change the outcome. I weigh most heavily the combination of a tractable model with predictions that micro-data can confirm or reject. Melitz (2003) predicts which firms export, why exporters differ systematically from non-exporters, and why liberalisation reallocates activity toward more productive firms. These implications are not generated by representative-firm trade models. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extends the logic to the choice between exporting and foreign direct investment, and the framework has been confronted with firm-level data in many countries for over twenty years. On the chair's question about wording, I would keep the citation to selection, reallocation and the gains from trade. It should not be a career citation for Helpman, and it should not claim all of quantitative trade. That wording leaves the Bernard-Jensen exporter facts, Eaton-Kortum and Hopenhayn to be acknowledged in the scientific background. On Redding, I would keep him out of the core. As I recall the literature, his main contribution is quantitative and spatial trade built on this base, and I have not heard any member give a specific contribution that makes him co-origin. A third name would also make the credit less clean. On the Pareto question, I understand the qualitative selection and reallocation result to be a property of heterogeneity combined with fixed export costs. It does not depend on one distribution. What does depend on the distributional assumptions is the size of the gains, and the citation should not rest on a welfare number. I am relying on recollection and have not independently verified this.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still credit. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and Hopenhayn are precursors or parallel contributors, and Redding is omitted. Narrow wording reduces this cost but does not remove it. The second reservation is that the size of the selection gains is sensitive to parametric assumptions. The third is whether the Committee accepts that this is distinct from the 2008 prize. I find the distinctness argument convincing, but Boppart's remaining hesitation shows it is not fully settled. As an empirical labour economist I also note that parts of the exporter-premium evidence are descriptive. Clean causal evidence on reallocation after liberalisation comes from a smaller set of episodes. Finally, B019 has a tighter single-mechanism attribution than B010, and I count that as a real advantage for B019.

responses.point: Boppart now treats B010 as a serious alternative but keeps B019 first. He argues that B019 has a tighter single-mechanism attribution with two clear originators, while B010 has real credit disputes over Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum. He stresses that this is a judgment between two strong candidates, not a claim that B010 is weaker on merit.
responses.response: I accept that Kiyotaki-Moore has the cleaner attribution, and I do not think B010 beats it on that criterion. The question is how much weight attribution should carry once both candidates have an identifiable core. For B010 the core is the selection-and-reallocation model, and the precursor facts motivated it without supplying it. That leaves a cost that careful citation wording and the scientific background can handle. The deciding consideration for me is the evidence. The B010 mechanism has been tested directly against firm-level register and customs data in many settings, while the collateral-amplification channel is identified more indirectly. If the Committee prefers B019, I would support Kiyotaki and Moore as a two-name award. I included Gertler in round 1 but would now drop him, for the 2022 overlap and the B037 credit problems you and others raised.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B019 first but is not fully settled on its order with B010. He argues that the 2022 prize rewarded work on banks and on runs and crises, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore concerns collateral values and asset-price feedback in the real economy. He also grants that B010 combines broad agreement with a clean attribution and a mature empirical record.
responses.response: That distinction answers much of the overlap concern for me. I do not think the 2022 prize makes B019 ineligible, and I would not use it to rank B019 below B010. Our remaining difference is about evidence, and it may be one of weighting. You rate a single identifiable mechanism and its thirty-year durability above a larger body of confirming data. I put more weight on direct empirical confrontation, which comes from my background in policy evaluation. Your own uncertainty about the order of B019 and B010 suggests this is a close call. That is why B019 is now my first alternative, ahead of B039 and B037. The Committee should test whether the amplification channel has been identified in data and not only shown to be influential.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B032 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She narrowed her set from Katz to Dorn to focus on the trade-shock core. She argues that a decade of scrutiny shows the findings were tested, and that continued debate over magnitudes is not evidence of fragility.
responses.response: I share your view that debate over magnitudes is a sign of scrutiny and not of fragility. The qualitative finding, that adjustment to import shocks is slow and costly, has survived re-examination. This is also close to my own field, so I disclose that proximity. My difficulty is that the shift-share exposure designs depend on identifying assumptions that are still being examined. The entry also bundles two strands, the China-shock empirics and the task and skill framework, and that bundling is what forced you to change your laureate set. I would not put B032 ahead of B010 on the common criteria. The conceptual framework in B010 is sharper and its predictions are more varied. I agree that B032 is a strong empirical programme. Which strand the Committee is rewarding would need to be settled before names can be fixed, and that is a harder attribution task than for B010.

responses.point: Krusell raises that trade was recognised in 2008, and in his case against B010 and in his later discussion he asks how much field balance (including the 2022 financial-crisis and 2024 institutions prizes) should weigh. He still treats B010 as scientifically large and as the cleanest attribution on his list.
responses.response: I agree with the chair's framing that field balance is a legitimate thing to disclose and discuss, but I would not let it decide between candidates on scientific merit. The common criteria are significance, attribution and maturity, and B010 does well on all three. If two candidates were genuinely tied, field balance could serve as a tiebreaker. Neither the 2022 nor the 2024 prize helps B010, because the argument against it is the 2008 trade prize, and I have argued that the contribution is distinct from that prize. The same reasoning applies to B039, where the 2024 prize is the closer neighbour. I gave that proximity too little weight in my opening ranking. This is part of why B019 now ranks above B039 among my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee accepts a two-name citation that omits Redding and the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum-Hopenhayn strand, and whether the scientific background can acknowledge those contributions adequately.

How much of the selection and reallocation result survives alternative productivity distributions. I believe the qualitative mechanism does and the magnitudes do not, but this is recollection and not verified.
Whether the Committee judges B010 distinct enough from the 2008 new trade theory prize. Boppart's hesitation shows the point is not unanimous.
Whether the evidence on direct identification should outweigh B019's cleaner two-name attribution. This is a close judgment and I could be underweighting the clean single mechanism.
My assessments are from recollection of the literature and the colleagues' files and are not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It documents no co-authorship or institutional tie with Helpman, Melitz, Kiyotaki, Moore or the other credited names on B010, B019 and B039. Its only documented overlap with Committee members is institutional, at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell), and that is not a co-authorship. Torsten Persson, credited on B039, is a past Committee member, which I note for disclosure only. My research field is empirical labour economics and policy evaluation, which is field-proximate to B032 and B012, though neither is in my configuration. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
